articles.content: US goes up 7-0 over El Salvador by half-time Win secures spot at 2027 World Cup and 2028 Olympics The United States’ place at a Women’s World Cup is treated as a foregone conclusion, but Friday’s all-or-nothing qualifier against El Salvador gave some reason for nerves. This was the first competitive game for Emma Hayes’ team since their Olympic gold medal match in August 2024, the end of two years of only friendlies. Given the global advances in women’s soccer over the years, maybe El Salvador could spring an all-time upset. The suspense ultimately lasted for eight minutes and 20 seconds. The USWNT opened the scoring in their Concacaf W Championship quarter-final with El Salvador in the ninth minute; a nifty training-ground set piece routine ending with Kennedy Wesley prodding the ball into the net, putting the hosts in the driver’s seat for an 8-0 win and a spot in next summer’s big show. With the win, the US maintains their perfect Women’s World Cup attendance record, a part of all 10 tournaments to date. Continue reading...

articles.content: A sensational start for the Italian was swiftly followed by a dismal run and long faces in the team This is the great known unknown in Manchester City’s run of one win – in addition to victory on penalties against Brighton in the Carabao Cup – in seven matches. After guilty verdicts were returned regarding the breaking of Premier League financial rules, Enzo Maresca’s team went to Anfield and handed Liverpool a 3-0 schooling . Yet this proved the falsest of dawns, with Andoni Iraola’s nascent side perhaps caught in a bad moment. City have since managed one league victory ( 3-2 over Ipswich , six days later) and two more wins in regulation time (in the Champions League) in 10 matches. The sequence includes one point from the past four league fixtures. Maresca argues that his, too, is an embryonic project so there will be uneven form. “I am not a magician,” he said on Friday. articles.content: There is cynicism and jealousy but one of County’s top scorers is 39 as club try to climb leagues again after tumbling It was a vidiprinter moment worthy of a double take. Don’t be silly, retorted County; four goals in the closing 17 minutes extended the Dingwall side’s goal difference to plus 45 (for 56, against 11). Played 16, won 14, drawn two. We lost a dubious goal, which shouldn’t have stood.” Earlier in that competition County whacked 14 past a Hearts youth side before defeating a Celtic B team including two Chelsea loanees and a £3m midfielder. articles.content: It’s early days, but after a dramatic roster overhaul and an offseason of team-bonding Dončić is playing at an MVP level and LA are looking like contenders One of the components of Luka Dončić’s shock trade from the Dallas Mavericks to the Los Angeles Lakers that caused great consternation was that he was just entering his prime as an NBA superstar. The worry was that the move could end that prime before it really even began – unceremoniously uprooting the Slovenian wunderkind from a team custom built around his strengths, fresh off a run to the NBA finals, to one who didn’t really make sense at all. Sure, the bright lights of Hollywood would elevate Dončić’s profile and usher him into a new echelon of stardom. But with Oklahoma City starting their run of dominance and rising stars around the league waiting in the wings, some believed his hopes of title contention (or even a long-elusive MVP award) had vanished. But the start to this season raises the question: what if they were wrong? Dončić is neck-and-neck with Victor Wembanyama in the MVP race, and the Lakers have the best record in the NBA at 15-3, with the Spurs and 76ers just behind at 15-4. San Antonio and their gargantuan French superstar were title and MVP favorites by a wide margin entering this season. But Dončić and the Lakers are keeping pace by pretty much every margin. Friday night’s NBA Cup showdown will be a duel with ripple effects and stakes rarely seen in the regular season, let alone in November. The two top records. The two leading MVP candidates. A basketball fan couldn’t ask for much more. Continue reading...

articles.content: Liam Delap can exploit Chelsea’s defensive woes while Senne Lammens is under pressure against Brentford Nottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. After they lost to Chelsea in October, a seventh defeat in 10 winless games, Forest’s form improved and they won seven of their next 12 in all competitions. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” Carragher concluded. articles.author: Ed Aarons at Selhurst Park
articles.content: Football seasons can pivot on certain moments and Thomas Frank will hope that Crystal Palace’s turning point came 17 minutes from full time here. Deservedly trailing to Mamadou Sarr’s goal having been second best throughout against Real Sociedad, this game – and perhaps the south London club’s entire trajectory – was turned on its head after Jon Martín was sent off for denying Jean-Philippe Mateta an equaliser. The France striker made no mistake with his penalty before Dwight McNeil – who made up for scoring an own goal in Saturday’s defeat by Coventry capped an extraordinary comeback in Frank’s first home match since succeeding Pierre Sage. Despite Yéremy Pino’s saved penalty in stoppage time and a number of other chances that were squandered, Dean Henderson pulled off a stunning late save to seal the victory and revive Palace’s Europa League campaign. Suddenly Palace have hope where there appeared to be none and the Premier League’s bottom side will head into Sunday’s crucial showdown with Hull with a spring in their step. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Bayern Munich’s 2-1 defeat to Lille was arguably the most eye-catching of Wednesday night’s Bigger Cup results, but anyone who tuned into proceedings at Stade Pierre-Mauroy will have been unsurprised by the outcome. Not so much an elite European tie as a game of Name That Bayern Reserve, the German champions’ starting lineup resembled a pale facsimile of its usual self. Their current knack-list includes such high-profile names as – deep breath – Harry Kane, Michael Olise, Alphonso Davies, Manuel Neuer, Serge Gnabry, Luis Díaz, Jamal Musiala and Ismael Saibari. And with Díaz and Musiala only fit enough for places on the bench, Konrad Laimer was deployed as a makeshift striker. The veteran right-back is famously as handy as a small pot, but filling Kane’s iconic Skechers proved a task too far for the Austrian. I liked Erling Haaland’s observation that football can simultaneously be “easy and difficult” [yesterday’s Football Daily]. That got me thinking about other things that have conflicting characteristics. Soup can be both sweet and sour. My feelings for my partner often run hot and cold. And my daily tea-timely newsletter can be mildly funny and mildly unfunny – Mike Wilner. The constant change in Watford manager, a once fine club whose first two managers lasted a total of 23 years, is now so high that I don’t even notice it anymore ... apparently this was yesterday, and I’ve no idea who the previous bloke was. Watford are now onto their 30th manager, including caretakers, although in practice they’re all just caretaker managers, since the Pozzos took over in 2012. I don’t know whether to laugh at, or cry for, the Watford fans (Narrator: it’s the former, obviously) – Noble Francis. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. articles.content: North Melbourne are out to secure their legacy but in their way stands a confident Melbourne side ready for their biggest test of the season The early chapters of the record books are still being written as the AFLW enters its second decade with North Melbourne now just one win away from a milestone that could stand the test of time. The Kangaroos have become the league’s benchmark during a dominant three seasons, and last year raised the bar higher as the first club to claim back-to-back premierships. A third consecutive grand final triumph when they face Melbourne at a sold out Ikon Park on Friday night would earn the Roos a larger slice of history – and cement their place as the competition’s first dynasty. The North Melbourne juggernaut has raised the standard of the AFLW; the Roos have lost only once since being defeated by Brisbane in the 2023 grand final, then turned the tables on the same rivals to win in the past two deciders. They romped through another campaign to finish the league’s 11th season as minor premiers with 11 victories and a percentage of 246.6%, though their record-breaking winning streak ended at 32 matches with a surprise loss to Hawthorn. articles.content: Unai Emery wanted the winger but, like Harvey Elliott last season, he has been left out in the cold despite Villa’s attacking struggles It is three years this week since Alejandro Garnacho opened the scoring for Manchester United in a 3-3 draw at Galatasaray in the Champions League, on a typically boisterous night in Istanbul when Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, now his teammates at Aston Villa, were also among the starters. At the time, Garnacho was a teenage star flourishing on the grandest of stages, a fixture in the United team and fresh from scoring an outrageous overhead kick at Goodison Park a few days earlier that would later clinch the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award. He went on to score twice at Old Trafford on Boxing Day, in a 3-2 victory against Villa, and a couple of months later his double at home to West Ham was the catalyst for that iconic celebration photo of Garnacho, Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund sitting on the advertising hoardings at the Stretford End, beaming smiles all round. All three were at the heart of United’s plans for a bright future, beacons of hope. At the end of that season, Garnacho signed off in style, he and Mainoo scoring against Manchester City at Wembley to win the FA Cup . Continue reading...

articles.content: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull, Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford. This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

The race to replace Australia’s No 3 – whether slotting straight into Labuschagne’s spot at first drop or as part of a batting order reshuffle – has become packed with Test discards and an emerging talent hoping to earn a debut. The door could open for more than one addition to the XI alongside presumed incumbents Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis and wicketkeeper Alex Carey, with worrying signs Australia’s ageing squad is starting to creak after three defeats in their past five Tests. articles.content: The job of Mauricio Pochettino’s successor is to fine-tune a team on the up. That requires a bureaucrat rather than a figurehead First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it. But let us assume that US Soccer can’t appoint Guardiola, because he is only a few months into his post-Manchester City sabbatical and still busying himself defending his body of work . Because he has given no recent indication that he wants the job, even though he spent a previous break between managerial gigs living in New York City and was probably only being supportive of his newly-appointed colleague Mauricio Pochettino when he called the project “fascinating” two years ago. Also because he has only ever signed on to coach teams stacked with Ballon d’Or contenders, posing a Phil Jackson-type, bar-room question over whether he would still be exceptional in charge of unexceptional players. Continue reading...

articles.content: A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979 Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio. Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer. Continue reading...

articles.author: Aaron Timms
articles.content: For big stars, endorsing companies like Kalshi and Polymarket is just another day in the beautiful business of being – and staying – rich When Giannis Antetokounmpo announced he was taking an investment stake in prediction market Kalshi in February, the claim he made to accompany the announcement – “We all on Kalshi now” – sounded as absurd as the howls of outrage from sports lovers seemed universal. Nine months later, Kalshi’s grip on American fans appears murderously tight: notional monthly trading volume on the platform, the majority of which is taken up by wagers on sports, increased to nearly $100bn in October from $40bn in August, as the company gears up for yet another funding round at a rumored valuation of $65bn ahead of a potential IPO. Rival prediction market Polymarket, which relaunched in the US late last year after regulators shut it down in 2022, has seen similar growth over recent months. However righteous the disgust from fans on social media at the deepening incursion of these odious platforms into professional sport may be, their popularity seems only to grow. More perplexing is the widening circle of athletes like Giannis who’ve thrown off whatever shame might once have come from association with these businesses and given them their full-throated support. The line between role model and shill in professional sports is now essentially non-existent. Pete Sampras, a man so private in retirement it can often seem like his entire tennis career was a collective hallucination, released an ad for Kalshi during this year’s US Open after two decades largely out of the public eye. José Mourinho trousered a brick of Kalshi cash this summer in exchange for a gambling promo during the World Cup. The prediction market machine now sponsors Jalen Brunson and Josh Hart’s Roommates Show, on which the recently crowned pair of NBA champions begin every episode dutifully informing us that their amazingly dreary podcast is “presented by Polymarket, the top prediction market”. LeBron James will make more from his recently announced partnership with Polymarket – $15m a year – than he will from playing for the Philadelphia 76ers. Somehow we’ve arrived at the point where it’s bigger news if a professional athlete takes a firm stand against the prediction markets, as Victor Wembanyama recently did , rather than pockets the cash to endorse them. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jonathan Wilson
articles.content: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered. Continue reading...

articles.content: Snapping a four-game losing streak, the Wallabies edged Wales in a performance that showed progress under Les Kiss The Wallabies had one per cent possession in the final ten minutes and still hung on to win. Those one percenters are exactly what Les Kiss is trying to rebuild after two blowout defeats to New Zealand, a bashing by England and a brutal beatdown by Scotland last week. Now, after entering the Dragon’s lair and silencing 75,000 Welsh, the rediscovery of such tiny tantalising margins is inching Australia back to their best By defeating Wales 26-29, the Wallabies have snapped their four-match losing streak and snatched their first win in eight northern hemisphere Tests to stay alive in the Nations Championship. Best of all, they did the little things that produce big results. This win has roused their self belief, restored the composure and creativity they had lost in attack, and given them a sniff of finishing a rollercoaster season on a high. Continue reading...

Justin Longmuir stood on the margins of the mayhem in Fremantle’s rooms last Friday night. His Dockers had mown down a willing but truncated Sydney side and Longmuir stood slouched, relieved, knackered. Some people walk into a room and automatically command it. Footy is full of people like that. Some are teachers. Some are generals who never found a war. Some, as Neale Daniher always said, are actors – projecting hope to the players and stability to the critics. Most of them are a bit mad. Longmuir has always been something of an outlier – a classic introvert who can come across as nervous and awkward in press conferences, a man who had to steel himself to speak to large groups when he started coaching. He’s not a coach who picks fights or creates diversions or speaks in riddles. He says he’s an over-thinker. He says he’s harder on himself than any critic, and there has been plenty of those. As one of just two senior coaches who have never played in or coached a grand final team, it’s something that can make him an easy target when the side are underperforming – that he doesn’t have the playing record, the aura, the eloquence, the polish, the prick in him.
